auckland: Auckland was naturally our first destination, where we intentionally stayed a couple of nights in a hotel to recover from jetlag before the actual campervan portion on the South Island. Auckland was a nice city and especially the harbor had lots to see. We found many good restaurants and with our luggage stuck in Los Angeles, it was good to do some shopping here. Generally, I wouldn't spend too much time in cities in New Zealand even though there's nothing wrong with them. There's just so much more to see in nature elsewhere.
waiheke: Waiheke Island exceeded all expectations. Just 40 minutes by ferry from Auckland, this paradise island offers world-class wineries, stunning beaches, and a relaxed Mediterranean vibe. The turquoise waters and golden sand beaches made us forget we were in the South Pacific.
waiheke-bike: eBikes were a great solution for getting around Waiheke Island. The bike rental shop provided a map and good directions for the route. The island had really beautiful houses and it was nice to cycle along the beaches looking at them. The island also has many wineries you can visit. Casita Miro winery had incredibly good tapas. We also visited an olive oil press. The cycling was also good practice for left-side traffic before starting to drive!
queenstown: Our campervan owner picked us up from Queenstown airport and we drove this route in his small car. The road was quite intense and for example the bus takes a different route between the towns. You could drive the road with a camper and there was one freedom camping spot along the route. It's apparently even dangerous in strong winds.
crown-range: Crown Range Road is one of New Zealand's most spectacular alpine drives. Climbing to 1,076 meters, the highest sealed road in the country, we were treated to jaw-dropping views of the mountains and valleys below. Every hairpin turn revealed a new panorama more stunning than the last.
wanaka: We picked up our campervan in Wanaka and didn't linger to explore the town but headed straight for our first hike, Roys Peak.
roys-peak: Physically one of the toughest hikes. It took us about 2h 15min to the summit with water breaks. Practically continuous climbing the whole way. We started the hike only after 5pm but made it back just as darkness fell. Definitely worth climbing all the way to the top! Descent is hard on the legs, takes the same time down as up.
red-bridge-camp: Freedom camping spots around Wanaka are scarce, so Red Bridge's large parking area was a fairly safe choice. The first time we arrived after dark and got the last free spot. The second time we arrived around 5pm and fit easily, but soon after us the place filled up and we watched all evening as campers had to turn away from the full lot. Two toilets, no other facilities.
queenstown-paknsave: This became our regular shop. Especially Queenstown's Pak N Save had a really good selection and cheap prices. Plus there was always wifi and toilets here, which you really appreciate when living in a camper!
te-anau: Full-service campground. Clean indoor facilities for cooking, laundry, and showers. Great location in Te Anau's center. We took a short evening walk by the lake and had a beer at the charming Redcliff Bar. We stayed here another night after returning from Fiordland.
lake-marian: Easy-ish route. The beginning is very easy with beautiful scenery along the river. Most of the trail runs through rainforest landscapes. The route ends at a lake surrounded by mountains.
lake-gunn: We did this hike as an evening walk from Cascade Creek campsite. A nice easy stroll, but definitely not worth going out of your way for.
cascade-creek: DOC campsite, meaning cheap and close to nature, no special facilities. Toilets and outdoor cooking shelter. No staff. One of the nicest overnight spots in terms of scenery and close to Fiordland hiking trails. It was freezing at night!
milford-sound: We went on a two-hour morning cruise and brought breakfast from the camper, knowing there would be free coffee on board! We got lucky with the weather as the day was sunny. Milford Sound gets rain about 200 days a year... The cruise guide told amusing stories in his unique style, which created a great atmosphere. Definitely worth the money and should be experienced. We also spotted seals lounging on the rocks. Allow plenty of time to arrive, as the road to Milford Sound is narrow and winding with lots of traffic. We left the car at the free parking lot, from where it's still a 20-minute walk to the ferry terminal. There was also a paid parking lot closer.
gertrude-saddle: One of the most stunning hikes — definitely worth going! We had planned to do this the same day as Lake Marian, but the weather was unstable. There are many warnings about weather on the route and it was a good idea to wait until the next day, when the weather was clear. The trail has difficult and rocky terrain with rock climbing, which is challenging when slippery. The views are amazing, so take advantage of clear weather. We got 'lucky' and there was still lots of snow on the trail. Most people didn't go to the end of the route because of it. Walking on snow worked well though and we could slide down. Allow plenty of time, food, and good clothes so you don't have to rush back.
queenstown-small-planet: Small Planet in Queenstown equipped us with everything needed for our backcountry camping adventure. Tents, sleeping bags, cooking gear — everything essential for a night under the stars near a glacier.
earnslaw-burn-parking: The Earnslaw Burn trailhead marks the beginning of one of New Zealand's hidden treasures. Parking among the beech trees, we prepared for our trek into a valley few visitors ever see.
earnslaw-burn: By far the toughest hike, but also by far the most beautiful. Many do this route as a day hike, but definitely worth staying overnight. The trail is very difficult and slow, especially with packs and overnight gear. This was the only route where we took considerably longer than the trail description said. The route has continuous ups and downs, fallen trees, and roots. Walking poles were absolutely essential here. There's one area on the trail where you can camp. It's not at the trail's end, but a few kilometers before it. We walked to the camping area for about 5.5 hours straight (in rain). We stayed overnight in the tent and after breakfast walked to the trail's end, about 1.5h each way. The route from the tent to the endpoint was very beautiful and the endpoint was one of the most stunning places we've visited. The endpoint was also a popular helicopter tour stop on good weather days, which didn't bother us. A couple who came to take wedding photos was quite a contrast to our scruffy hiking look. Allow plenty of time for this (if planning to walk the whole route the same day, there isn't time). On the way back, we picked up our gear and trudged back another 5.5 hours.
queenstown-camp: Back in Queenstown after our backcountry adventure, we appreciated the simple comforts of a proper campsite. Hot showers never felt so good after days in the wilderness.
arrowtown: Full-service campground. Good cooking facilities outdoors too. Many long-term guests. Arrowtown's cute village was within walking distance and we could have spent a bit more time there. The terraces looked lively and there were several restaurants that surely would have suited us. This time we went with the ice cream strategy and spent the rest of the day celebrating Christmas Eve at our accommodation.
lake-tekapo: Lake Tekapo's impossibly turquoise waters are fed by glacial flour from the nearby mountains. We spent hours walking along the shores, marveling at the color that seems too vivid to be real. The Church of the Good Shepherd provided a perfect frame for this natural masterpiece.
mackenzie-rv-camp: Very basic parking lot. One toilet, no other facilities.
tekapo-spa: Lounging in Tekapo's hot pools with views of the turquoise lake and snow-capped mountains was pure bliss. The contrast of warm water and cool mountain air, combined with that incredible view, created a perfect moment of relaxation.
lake-pukaki: Huge parking area with multiple 'levels'. Toilets quite far away (about 0.5km) if you choose the furthest parking spot. Beautiful scenery but very windy and partly uneven terrain. The only place where we saw inspectors checking that everyone has permitted campers.
mt-cook: Aoraki/Mount Cook, at 3,724 meters, is New Zealand's highest peak. The village at its base serves well as a starting point for multiple hikes.
sealy-tarns: Almost the entire trail was climbing stairs. The stairs were mostly in good condition, but the climb is tough. The climb was however considerably faster than the trail description. This was a very popular route, probably the most crowded after Tongariro Crossing. Sometimes had to wait on the stairs for people coming the other way to pass. Great views from the endpoint in good weather. You can continue the same route to Mueller Hut and stay overnight (must book in advance). The Hooker Valley trail also starts from the same parking lot, which was closed during our trip. The parking lot is paid and very full because the trails are popular.
blue-lakes: We did this route after Sealy Tarns. Very easy and quick trail. Very popular and the parking lot was packed with tourists. We also had a lunch break at the parking lot after the walk.
chamberlains-ford: Campground where the back section has mostly only long-term guests. We happened to park next to such a group and they were very noisy people. Britney Spears was their karaoke favorite. A river runs alongside where it was nice to eat breakfast. Lots of toilets, no other facilities.
christchurch: We only made a quick visit to Christchurch, but managed to explore a nice market hall with lots of different food stalls and small boutiques. The market hall was really cozy and we could have spent more time there. We walked back to the car through the botanical garden, which was part of a larger park area. Definitely worth visiting.
akaroa: The only freedom camping nearby, so it fills up quickly. We arrived early afternoon and got a spot, but it filled up quickly after that. Harbor parking with a bit of a walk to toilets (about 300m). The center was right next to the harbor, so a really good location to explore this charming village. The famous lighthouse is on the other side of the center, but even there it's only a few kilometers. Definitely try the best fish & chips in the center from a small cart and grab real fruit ice cream for dessert from the cart next to it! The next morning we had breakfast in the center and got pastries from a bakery called A la baguette and ate them at the café next door, from which we only ordered coffee and smoothies. This seemed to be a common practice. The pastries especially were really good!
akaroa-kayaking: The guided kayak trip had about 10 people. There were also complete beginners which affected the pace somewhat. The trip stayed around the harbor area anyway. We got really lucky with the weather, but trips were also run in pouring rain. We didn't see animals on our trip, but the guide told really interesting things about sea plants and we found various seaweed, mussels, and starfish.
bealey-spur: Very easy trail. A couple of nice viewpoints along the way. Quick to walk and at a brisk pace we arrived at the destination much faster than the guides said. At the end is a very old and basic hut where at least one group was staying overnight. There were also toilets and a fire pit at the end. A nice route for exercise.
devils-punch-bowl: We did this route after Bealey Spur. We set off unprepared in flip-flops and the trail was surprisingly tough because of the stairs. The route isn't long, but you should still wear proper shoes. A beautiful waterfall at the end.
jacksons: Small campground, good showers and cooking facilities. Option to do a hike to a waterfall and you can see glowworms in the yard after dark.
franz-josef: The West Coast wasn't originally on our route, but since we had time and one Finnish friend of ours lived in Franz Josef, we had to visit. A really charming small village that's easy to explore on foot. Relative to its small size, it had lots of restaurants and pubs, which suited our recovery day activities. From here it would be easy to take a helicopter flight to several different glaciers.
orange-sheep: A rainforest-terrain camping in the village center. Good showers and cooking facilities. Also a hot tub area next door, which is surely nice after a hike.
alex-knob: Long hike, but surprisingly easy compared to the trail description. The route was very clear and easy to walk. There are a few viewpoints along the way and from the summit views to the glacier, sea, and village. On the way back, you can do a small extra loop to a nearby pond if you have energy left. Very few parking spots at the trailhead. We left before 8am and still fit, but after that you have to take the car about a kilometer away to paid parking.
brewster-trailhead: Not a permitted overnight spot. Besides us, lots of cars in the parking lot but no other overnighters. From the parking lot you can go see the river crossing and waterfall at the start of the trail. When we returned from the hike, the parking lot was packed with tourists who came to see the waterfall.
brewster-hut: The trail started with a river crossing, which isn't possible during high water, but on our hike it was a pleasant and refreshing experience. After this, the hike was practically 5km straight up steep terrain. The route was relatively clear despite being roots and rocks all the way up. At the top was a beautiful hut and we regretted not booking overnight here in time. From the hut it would be another good hour to the glacier, but the weather was cloudy and rain starting, so we decided to turn back. Staying at the hut and walking to the glacier in the morning in good weather would surely have been an amazing experience. The way down was tougher and more challenging than going up. Knees always take a beating from hours of continuous stepping downward. Highly recommend this hike, but good weather is important.
blue-pools: We did this easy walk after the Brewster track and it's an accessible few-kilometer walk to a beautiful swimming spot in a glacier river pool. Because the route was so easy and started right from the road, the place was also quite full of tourists. Definitely go swimming at the endpoint after admiring the crystal-clear river from the suspension bridge. The water is naturally cold, but a swim-worthy destination.
red-bridge-camp-return: Returning to Red Bridge felt like coming home. The familiar campsite welcomed us back, and we reflected on the incredible journey through the glaciers and mountains of the West Coast.
wanaka-center: Wanaka is a popular tourist town. The center has lots of shops, restaurants, and bars. There was a nice food truck area with good food. After dropping off the camper, we traveled from Wanaka to Queenstown by bus, which was a really fun experience. The driver was a proper tour guide and we stopped at local markets for shopping, ice cream, and bathroom break, even though the trip only took about 1.5 hours.
hampshire-wanaka: After dropping off the camper, we continued the caravan lifestyle and stayed overnight in Wanaka at a campground. It was quite luxurious to stay in a small cabin overnight. Toilets and showers were still shared though. Accommodations in Wanaka were really booked and when booking online everything looked full or really expensive. By calling, we managed to book this small cabin at a very reasonable price.
queenstown-explore: Queenstown is New Zealand's 'adventure capital'. There are lots of tourists and campervan-living people here. When going by camper, think well in advance where you'll stay overnight. We came from the Earnslaw Burn hike late in the evening to town, not realizing that every freedom camping and paid camping in town had been booked long ago. We had to drive around only to find we didn't fit anywhere. We were about to go to Pak N Save's parking lot (prohibited, 400€ fine) for the night when we noticed the airport's paid parking area. We went there, although you probably weren't allowed to stay overnight there either. We left early in the morning and our short visit only cost 4€. Queenstown is busy and touristy, but a fun place to wander around for a day. Fergburger is the country's most famous burger place. Allow at least an hour for queuing regardless of time, probably more. We also went to a wine bar where you could order tastings from self-service taps from hundreds of different wines. Queenstown Gardens was also a nice area. Getting hiking gear rental in Queenstown was very easy, so if you need it, do the rental here. Our very high-quality rental gear (tent, sleeping bags, sleeping pads, camp stove, and walking poles) cost about 70€ total for one overnight trip. If you want to stay overnight at huts, you need your own sleeping bag, so consider renting one for a longer period.
black-sheep: Black Sheep Backpackers in Queenstown provided a base for our last night on the South Island. The hostel atmosphere was relaxed and as a bonus there was a sauna + hot tub combo in the backyard.
wellington: We spent a day in Wellington in a probably typical tourist way. First went along Cuba Street toward the harbor and ate along the way. Must say that having been to Cuba, the street had nothing Cuban about it except the name. The harbor was nice to hang out at and we even saw a stingray in the harbor basin. After this we took the famous Cable Car up to the botanical garden to see the views and finally back down to the center to eat and then it was time to head to our next accommodation for the evening.
porirua: Really cute 'treehouse-like' Airbnb. Unfortunately we were here just to sleep and didn't have time to explore the area more. The Airbnb host had good tips for nearby areas and it seemed like a nice place!
powell-hut-trailhead: There would also be a campground next to the trailhead if you wanted to stay overnight at the starting point.
powell-hut: Our first hike on the North Island. The route was mostly very easy to walk: flat, gentle uphill, and even downhill. Only the end of the route had steep climbing, much of which was stairs so quite easy to walk. The hut came up surprisingly quickly. The hut was really cute and a nice place to have a snack break. You could also stay overnight here (must book in advance). You could continue the route to the mountaintop or also onward to a different trail. This was the only place where we ran into Finns (living in New Zealand)!
hastings: The first place where we stayed two nights in a row. Our Airbnb was at Zaria Wines winery owners' place. A really nice small winery that's also their home. The owner held a wine tasting for us on our own terrace and had left a welcome bottle of their own wine. The wines were excellent and we bought some to take home. He also advised us about other wineries in the area. Otherwise the area didn't have much to see.
hastings-golf: The morning golf round in Hastings was a nice change from hiking. The course was in mint condition and we found nice local playing company. There are golf courses in every village in New Zealand, so for those interested in golf, bring your clubs.
hastings-wine: The area is known for wineries and there are many. Distances are quite long though, so you have to go by car or bike. Not all estates have tastings and tastings are only open 11am-5pm, so keep that in mind when planning visits. Some estates also have restaurants, but not all.
waimarama: Super fun experience! We took a private surfing lesson. The beach was really good and calm for beginners and the waves were really good.
napier: We only stopped in Napier for a quick lunch break and looked at the beach a bit. It surely would have been a nice place to spend more time, but on the other hand the entire east coast of the North Island is full of similar beaches.
taupo: Taupo is located on the shore of New Zealand's largest lake. The town was surprisingly nice and lively. Naturally hot springs were the thing here too. Hot water beach is definitely worth trying. You can drive right up to it and it's a bewildering feeling when your feet sink into hot sand, but otherwise the water is regular cool lake water.
spa-park: We happened to have a really beautiful summer day, so the only right choice was to spend it by the river sunbathing. What made this river special was one of its pools, into which a couple of hot streams flowed. This created a natural hot tub, which was a nice experience combined with the cool river. Many locals went by floating on various beach toys and that surely would have been a fun experience.
turangi: Turangi served as our base for the Tongariro Crossing. There's not much more to say about this place, but it was a good place to stay before the hike.
tongariro-start: The Mangatepopo car park at dawn was buzzing with excitement. Hikers from around the world prepared for what many call New Zealand's greatest day walk, and we were among them.
tongariro: Tongariro Alpine Crossing is the most popular day hike, and you notice it. We bought bus tickets in advance from the trail endpoint to the starting point and set off around 8am. The route is reasonably easy to walk. The scenery is really beautiful, but the crowds compared to other routes were intense. The distance is over 20km, but wasn't among the most challenging. It was nice that from the trail endpoint we could leave immediately in our own car without waiting for a bus, so we recommend doing the route this direction.
rotorua: You notice Rotorua's geothermal activity as soon as you arrive in town. The sulfur smell, steaming pools, and bubbling mud are the town's trademarks. We visited a geothermal area to see hot springs and mud pools.
kaituna-cascades: Definitely worth doing! The rafting was done in groups of six plus a guide. We went down many waterfalls, the highest being 7 meters, the world's highest commercially rafted waterfall. We also got to swim in the current and go down one waterfall swimming. The water was quite warm and you get a wetsuit. A really intense and fun experience!
mt-maunganui: As our trip was ending, we had climbed so many mountains that summiting Mount Maunganui no longer excited us. So we did the few-kilometer circuit around the mountain instead, which is a popular jogging route. Very easy to walk, but surprisingly beautiful! Really nice scenery of the sea the whole route. A couple weeks after our visit, there was a bad landslide in the area where people died.
tairua: This was the second place on the trip where we stayed two nights in a row. Tairua's Airbnb was the best of our trip: stunning views, modern apartment, and very friendly hosts. Tairua was a really charming small village where you could get Real Fruit Ice Cream from several places! There was also an excellent pizza cart here.
pinnacles-trailhead: The Pinnacles trailhead marked the start of our last major hike in New Zealand. The forest here is special — kauri trees tower overhead, survivors of a time when dinosaurs roamed.
pinnacles: Our last hike. You had to drive a long way on mountain roads from the other side of the peninsula from Tairua to reach the trailhead. The road to the trailhead was really narrow and in poor condition. The hike to Pinnacles Hut was easy-ish and there were many children and dogs on the trail too. Pinnacles Hut is huge, an 80-person hut that must be booked in advance. Very popular and touristy, so not the best hut for overnight stays. From the hut there was still climbing to the actual Pinnacles summit, but overall the route was at least half as fast as described. On the way back, we chose to come back via a different route instead of the same way. That was a mistake, as the route had nothing much to see and was too hard on our trip-worn knees with its ups and downs. This return route was also much longer and/or slower than the way there.
sailors-grave: Our Airbnb host tipped us about a nearby beach known only to locals. We left the car at another beach's (which was also beautiful) parking lot and walked about 15 minutes on a rough trail to a beach that was a true paradise.
auckland-airport: The rental car was returned at Auckland Airport and then we were ready to head home via Doha.
home: Back home and planning the next trip...
